old_text: \abstract{Marketing teams evaluate promotions using recorded sales, but stockouts hide demand. Naive-versus-corrected comparisons can confound censoring correction with covariate and link changes. We develop a matched specification audit and complementary simulation stress tests. Applied to FreshRetailNet-50K (50,000 store-product series, 90 days), the matched censored-versus-observed Poisson contrast across 254 city-category panels has median gaps of 25.3\% for the discount-depth coefficient and 52.4\% for the promotion-indicator coefficient; 59.8\%/77.2\% of panels exceed a 20\% disclosure threshold. These gaps are smaller than the 50.2\%/84.1\% unmatched benchmark. In the tested nonzero shared-shock settings, Poisson recovery has higher coefficient-estimation error than observed-sales estimators. The empirical gaps are associational and relative to a Poisson recovery model, not errors against latent demand; some alternatives have convergence limitations. We recommend reporting observed and recovered estimates together as a sensitivity comparison rather than substituting recovered estimates unconditionally.}

old_text: \emph{Stockout days with no lost demand.} A day on which stock runs out only after the day's demand has been met has $K = D$, yet the flag marks it as censored. Under A2 the contribution $1 - F(K;\lambda)$ then treats $D > K$ as certain, which would overstate lost demand. A small tail probability does not imply a small log-likelihood contribution: $\log\Pr(D>K)$ becomes more negative as the tail probability decreases. For integer Poisson demand and integer $K$, $E[D\mid D>K]-K\geq1$, so the imposed shortfall cannot approach zero. The strict-censoring likelihood does not accommodate a flagged day with no lost demand; an explicit observation model is needed. The reverse problem is also present: the pilot cell shows 15.1\% of all-day-stockout days with some recorded sales and some stockout hours with positive sales, so the flag is a noisy lower-bound indicator rather than a reliable record of lost demand (\S\ref{sec:4-1}). A mixture likelihood in which a flagged day is truly censored with probability $\pi<1$, contributing $\pi\,[1-F(K;\lambda)] + (1-\pi)\,f(K;\lambda)$, has been estimated at fixed $\pi=0.95/0.85/0.75$ and with $\pi$ estimated per cell (Appendix~\ref{app:recovery}). Mixture fits yield similar gaps where they converge, with convergence limitations; the primary estimates remain conditional on treating every flagged day as censored.

One scenario breaks it: A4, where the stockout capacity ceiling is driven by the same latent shock as demand itself: i.e., the \emph{timing} of a stockout, not just its frequency, carries information about unobserved demand that neither the recovery model M, nor the distributional alternatives NB2/MIX, account for. Once the shared-shock strength exceeds the boundary (ignorable) case, all three correction methods have higher median relative error than naive/G at every tested $\rho$, formally hypothesis-tested only for M (8/8 Holm-significant at $\rho=0.5/1.0$; full test counts, effect sizes, and the fit-level coefficient-error rate are reported in \S\ref{sec:3-10} and are not repeated here).
new_text: \S\ref{sec:3-10}'s benchmark found M robust to misspecified demand distributions and censoring-label noise (A0--A3). A4 differs: when the capacity ceiling is driven by the same latent shock as demand, the tested generator censors nearly every day once $\rho>0$, and the censored-Poisson likelihood then typically has no finite maximum (structural non-existence in 2,080 and 2,442 of 2,700 datasets at $\rho=0.5/1.0$). This non-existence, not a finite-sample error of a computed estimate, is the demonstrated failure mode; NB2 and MIX fail at equal or higher rates. Where a finite MLE exists, the M-versus-naive/G comparison is mixed (Table~\ref{tab:e2a4}).

new_text: \textbf{Scope, stated precisely.} This is a failure under one generative construction (a shared latent shock linking demand and capacity), not a general law. old_text: \textbf{Decision rule and what it actually shows.} The 25.3\%/52.4\% medians would be said to \emph{survive} an alternative if, under it, the median gap is at least 20\% and the share of cells above 20\% is at least 50\% for the coefficient in question, with the lower bound of the cluster interval above 20\%, computed on the cells where that alternative actually converges. Under that correct reading, NB2 and ZIP convergence is too sparse (16 and 9 of 254 cells) to apply the rule with any power: the NB2 converged-subset CI straddles the threshold and the ZIP converged-subset median falls below it (previous paragraph). We therefore do not claim the rule is satisfied under NB2 or ZIP, and we do not use either to adjust the Poisson-M gap up or down. The fixed-probability mixture-censoring (label-noise) alternatives converge in 87--168/254 cells and are reported as sensitivity checks with convergence limitations; NB2 and ZIP are reported as a model-selection-sensitivity audit finding in their own right: the low convergence rate is evidence that model comparison here is itself fragile, which is exactly the kind of instability the paper's diagnostic workflow (\S\ref{sec:3-4}) is designed to surface rather than paper over. The recommendation is to report both estimates conditional on the Poisson model, with convergence limitations for the sensitivity fits (\S\ref{sec:4-13}).
